title: Evolution of heat tolerance and drug resistance in Cryptococcus
text:
Many pathogens live in the environment prior to encountering a mammalian host. As a result, human
interactions with the environment can alter the population of pathogens we are likely to encounter and thus
with which we are infected. This proposal aims to understand how heat tolerance and drug resistance are
controlled by genetic variation at two different time scales (across a genus and within a species) of
opportunistic environmental fungal pathogens in order to better predict how pathogens are likely to be altered
by human activities.

title: Glial-mediated synaptic remodeling in drug addiction
text:
Increasing evidence suggests that astrocytes play a critical role in regulating synaptic plasticity and circuit
remodeling, but their role in addiction-related cellular and behavioral adaptations remains underexplored. The
current application aims to understand astrocyte-mediated remodeling of cocaine-generated synapses and
neuronal populations that drive cocaine seeking. The expected results will provide new insights into novel
mechanisms underlying drug addiction.

title: Treatment for Medication-related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw in Rice Rats via In Situ Delivery of an Anti-Inflammatory Enzyme with Spatial Metabolome/Glycome Profiling of Disease Progression and Therapy
text:
This proposal will investigate a novel therapeutic strategy for Medication-related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw
(MRONJ) by locally delivering an engineered IDO-Gal3 fusion protein to the primary lesion site. We aim to
reduce MRONJ incidence by modulating local inflammation, generating anti-inflammatory metabolites, and
shifting the metabolic and glycomic profiles towards healthy states at the lesion site. Our goal is to establish a
robust preclinical foundation for effective MRONJ treatment, ultimately enhancing patient health and well-
being.

title: Microbiology of Treatment Shortening in Tuberculosis
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – PROJECT 3 Despite the availability of antibiotics to treat tuberculosis (TB) for over 70 years, TB remains the single leading cause of death due to infectious disease. The prolonged treatment required to prevent a high relapse rate is one of the main reasons why TB remains a significant public health concern. Prolonged TB treatment is required for numerous reasons, important among them being poor intralesional pharmacokinetics (PK) and poor intralesional pharmacodynamics (PD). Shortening the duration of TB treatment is a central goal in TB drug discovery. One proposed route to shortening the length of TB treatment is to leverage drug target interactions to improve regimen PD. To address this issue, we will use innovative, CRISPR-based methods in Mtb to identify optimal drug-target combinations that have the potential to sterilize the causative agent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in vitro and in vivo. Drug regimens developed based on this knowledge could contribute to faster TB cure. To identify highly efficacious Mtb drug-target combinations, we will leverage CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) based genetic- interaction (GI) mapping. GI mapping involves the pairwise measurement of how the inhibition of one gene modulates the phenotype of another gene. Applied broadly across many pairs of functionally diverse genes, GI maps provide a signature of interactions for each gene that act as a high-resolution, quantitative phenotype. In the field of cancer biology, GI maps are increasingly being used to inform rational design of effective cancer chemotherapy combinations. This project seeks to take a similar approach to optimize TB therapies. Here, we will develop an atlas of GI maps in Mtb that will enable the identification of target combinations that are fundamentally anchored in Mtb’s physiologic vulnerabilities, and are also compatible with new and existing drugs. These data, in combination with the other Projects and Cores, will provide the opportunity to discover and test potentially ‘universal’ target combinations that may be condition and/or subpopulation-independent.

title: Lung Allograft Stem Cell Regeneration and Immune Destruction
text:
Lung transplantation is often the best remaining treatment option for patients with end-stage
lung disease, but immune rejection can limit long-term survival. We must address major knowledge gaps in how
airway cells are renewed in lungs after transplantation and how the recipient's immune system targets and
destroys airway stem cells. Thus, there is a critical need to develop and use appropriate animal models to study
the destruction of stem cells in the lung.

title: Causes and Consequences of Preschooler's Digital Media Use: The Role of Sleep, Physical Activity, Sedentary Behavior and Social Emotional Health
text:
Children spend more time than ever using screens — increasingly on portable digital media devices like tablets
and smartphones, but our understanding about how these devices impact health is lagging. This project
proposes to uncover how patterns of digital media use are formed and maintained and examine how those
patterns predict mental health and cardiovascular health risk over time. The novel forms of media measurement
used in this project – including passive mobile sampling, ecological momentary assessment and accelerometry
– will allow us to uncover the unique and complex ways in which digital media impacts health behaviors.

title: Probing Tissue Heterogeneity and Stem Cell Niche with Micro-Organospheres
text:
Stem cells differentiate into various cell lineages to form tissues that perform many functions, but current in vitro
models do not capture tissue heterogeneity. This project will leverage Micro-OrganoSpheres (MOS) to develop
a high-throughput screen to understand host-microbe interaction, a combinatorial indexing technique to probe
local cell-cell interactions, and chimeras to study cell fate decisions and stem cell niche progression.

title: Scalable, Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML)- Driven Integration and Interrogation to Modernize the STEP Pediatric Excipient Database
text: The objective of the Resource to Advance Pediatrics and HIV Prevention Science contracts is to provide the extramural scientific community with research materials and preclinical product development support for candidate products that emerge from investigator-initiated research studies, or from collaborations with private sector or academic partners. These services may also be used to support product discovery and development leading to IND, Investigational Device Exemption (IDE), and/or New Drug Application (NDA) filings with the FDA. NIAID will primarily use these contracts to fill critical development and resource gaps more rapidly and efficiently and advance promising products into clinical testing. The focus of these contracts will be development of therapeutics and prevention products for HIV, including single or combination products with activity against associated co-infections or MPTs that incorporate contraceptives. This task order is to support scalable, reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML)- driven integration and interrogation to modernize the Safety and Toxicity of Excipients for Pediatrics (STEP) Database.

title: Aberrant proteomes in tauopathy: revealing functional consequences via multimodal proteomics
text:
Pathological tau species are a predominant hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease, however we lack a systematic
understanding of the functional consequences for the proteome and the role in disease progression. Here we
propose to use a proteogenomic approach to comprehensively map the impact of tau pathology on disrupting
the proteome with cell type, subcellular, and molecular resolution. These results will deepen our understanding
of functional mechanisms driving Alzheimer’s disease and have the potential to pinpoint novel therapeutic
targets.

title: Determining susceptibility loci in triple negative breast cancer using a novel pre-clinical model
text:
This proposal utilizes a novel model of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) which has been
created by systematically crossing a spontaneous model of TNBC into the BXD family, the largest and best
characterized murine genetic reference population, to discover and validate genetic modifiers of tumor
aggression and response to therapy. The BXD-TNBC hybrids demonstrate significant, heritable variation in
tumor phenotypes which have yielded candidate genes using systems genetics and cross-species
comparisons of existing human databases. The generation of this reliable, reproducible, and robust resource
will enable the discovery of genetic and environmental modifiers which will be leveraged to further understand
TNBC to maximally improve patient outcomes.

title: Investigating the Role of GZMA-Producing Tissue-Resident Memory Th17 Cells in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), which includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, affects more than 3
million people in the United States, causing long-term gut problems like pain, diarrhea, and tissue damage, and
current treatments don’t help everyone. This project will study a special type of immune cell in the gut, called
Trm17 cells, that makes a protein called granzyme A (GZMA), which can harm the gut lining. By learning how
these cells cause gut damage, this research could help find better treatments to reduce inflammation and
improve life for people with IBD, supporting the NIH’s goal to improve health and tackle serious diseases.

title: Neurogenesis in the adult Drosophila brain
text:
It would be advantageous to be able to treat neurodegenerative diseases and brain injuries using cells resident
in the brain as versus transplanted stem cells. We have developed a novel neurogenesis paradigm in the adult
brain of the genetic model organism Drosophila melanogaster and are using this model to explore the
molecular mechanisms underlying brain regeneration. The goals of the experiments proposed in this
application are to elucidate the role of glia cells in facilitating neurogenesis and to identify signaling pathways
that trigger the regenerative cascade. Because of the extensive genetic parallels underlying Drosophila and
mammalian brain development, we anticipate that our discoveries will be clinically relevant.

title: The genomic landscape and evolution of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
text:
Compared to other cancer subtypes with similar incidences, mortalities, and economic burdens, little is known
about the genetic landscape and evolution of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. For this grant, we will
address these gaps in knowledge. Completion of these studies will overcome major obstacles that are
currently hindering the development of new therapies and prevention strategies.

title: Efficient Delivery of Optimized Painless Nerve Growth Factors to the Central Nervous System to Treat Spinal Cord Injuries
text:
Although nerve growth factor (NGF) is a promising pharmacological strategy to treat spinal cord injuries, its
application is hindered by its large molecular size, high polarity, insufficient penetration into the spinal cord, and
induced nociceptor response. These limitations have been corrected by validated technologies from each
institution in this multi-disciplinary collaboration. In this proposal, the research consortium combine these
technologies and synthesizes a novel double-encapsulation system, denoted as des-n(NGFp) and will test its
therapeutic efficacy in a mouse spinal cord injury model.

title: Single-Cell Dissection of Cellular and Transcriptional Dynamics Driving Post-Transplant Relapse in Myelodysplastic Syndromes
text:
The proposed research is highly relevant to public health as it aims to improve the outcomes of allogeneic
hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, a life-saving treatment for patients with myelodysplastic syndromes
(MDS). By uncovering T cell phenotypes, clonal dynamics, and gene signatures linked to posttransplant relapse,
and elucidating their interplay with MDS-associated somatic mutations, this study will inform personalized
relapse prevention strategies. Ultimately, the findings could enhance patient survival, reduce healthcare burden,
and improve the quality of care for individuals undergoing transplantation.

title: Precision electrophysiology using multimodality imaging
text:
Cardiac arrhythmias affect more than 5% of patients in the United States and increases mortality and
morbidities. Novel multi-modality imaging in echocardiography, computed tomography, magnetic
resonance imaging can enable precision understanding of arrhythmic mechanisms and improve
delivery of therapeutic treatment such as ablation. We propose a patient oriented research study and
mentoring program to train young investigators to study the use of multimodality imaging to understand
alterations in myocardial thickness, tissue substrate, and electromechanical coupling in isthmus areas
and areas of triggered activity that can lead to arrhythmogenesis.

title: Defining the Mechanism of Genome Rearrangements in Ph-Like ALL to Determine Predictive Markers in High-Risk Hispanic Populations
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on genetic and epigenetic factors that
underlie the etiology of Ph-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia where there exists a cancer health disparity within
the Hispanic/Latino population regarding incidence, prevalence, and mortality. Further understanding of these
factors lays the groundwork for predictive diagnostics and personalized preventative medicine. Thus, this
proposal is relevant to the part of the NIH’s mission to foster discoveries pertaining to the causes, diagnosis, and
prevention human diseases and improve human health.

title: Structurally Decoding the Biosynthetic Logic of Modular Polyketide Synthases
text:
This MIRA proposal takes aim at modular type I polyketide synthases (PKSs) in bacteria responsbile for
biosynthesis of complex and medicinally important natural products. Understanding the mechanisms of modular
PKS operation could be harnessed to genetically encode the biosynthesis of user-defined small molecules. To
unlock programmable biosynthesis of new medicines, we will develop and apply our unique blend of structure-
function tools for resolving critical macromolecular structures and dynamics of a natural antibiotic-producing PKS
assembly line.

title: Study of Alzheimer's Disease Risk Genes Using Blood-Brain Barrier Assembloids
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no cure, and emerging
evidence suggests that early blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction contributes to disease onset and progression.
This project aims to develop and apply a novel human iPSC-derived BBB assembloid platform, genetically
engineered with Alzheimer’s-associated risk variants, to define the molecular mechanisms by which these
variants drive BBB breakdown. By uncovering how AD genetic risk disrupts neurovascular function, this work will
inform future therapeutic strategies targeting the BBB and support public health efforts to prevent or delay
cognitive decline in aging populations.

title: Determining the contribution of microbial-derived metabolites to protective immunity in obesity-driven cancer risk.
text:
Obesity is broadly associated with both increased incidences of a variety of cancers and a chronic
inflammatory state. Our interdisciplinary team with expertise in cancer, obesity, microbiome,
immunometabolism will test if obesity-altered gut microbes enhance cancer risk through dysregulated
protective immunity which leads to changes in the immune milieu that increase cancer cell transformation and
initiation. These studies will increase understanding of obesity-associated cancer risk and point to potential
interventions to alleviate this risk or treat existing cancers.
